purpose: Check a short library-rule derivation line by line, then compare its syntactic justification with truth in a selected situation.
meaning: A formal derivation is a finite sequence whose lines are premises or follow from earlier lines by declared inference rules. Here a small forward calculus uses premise membership and modus ponens. A valid candidate witnesses derivability from Γ; truth under one assignment, semantic entailment and the correctness of a particular written candidate remain separate questions.

definition.setting: A fixed three-premise propositional calculus with three selectable five-line candidates, the target r and all eight Boolean assignments.
definition.formal_latex: \Gamma=\{p,p\to q,q\to r\},\quad\frac{A\qquad A\to B}{B}\;\mathrm{MP},\quad\Gamma\vdash r,\quad\Gamma\models r.

signature.p: The return is recorded; a proposition with a selected-world truth value.
signature.q: The count is updated; a proposition with a selected-world truth value.
signature.r: The receipt is ready; the target proposition.
signature.k: Number of candidate lines currently revealed.
signature.v: The selected Boolean assignment to p,q,r.
signature.⊢: Syntactic derivability in the stated premise-and-modus-ponens calculus.
signature.⊨: Semantic entailment: no true-premises, false-conclusion assignment.
signature.MP: Modus ponens: infer B from A and A→B.

conditions: The fixed premise set, or assumption set, is Γ={p,p→q,q→r}. In the constructed library story, p means the return is recorded, q means the count is updated, and r means the receipt is ready. These rules are stipulated premises, not measured software guarantees.

A candidate has five ordered lines. A premise line must belong to Γ. Each line citation in a modus ponens step must identify one of two earlier accepted lines containing A and A→B, and its conclusion must be B.

The chain candidate writes p, p→q and q→r as its first three lines, then derives q from lines 1 and 2 and r from lines 4 and 3. The other candidates contain an incorrect conclusion or a future-line citation at line 4.
Only a consecutive valid prefix is accepted. Checking stops accepting new lines at the first invalid line; a later correct line does not repair the rejected candidate prefix.

The known chain witnesses Γ⊢r in this stated forward calculus. All eight Boolean assignments also verify Γ⊨r: no assignment makes every premise true and r false. A bad candidate does not refute the existence of this other valid derivation.

The selected world v is a valuation supplying truth values for p,q,r. Changing it affects truth readings and premise satisfaction, not whether a syntactic step obeys the proof rules. A derivation from Γ does not assert that Γ describes the actual library.
definition.domain_notes: The checker handles only three stated candidates in a tiny premise-and-modus-ponens calculus. It is not a complete propositional proof system, an arbitrary theorem prover or a proof of soundness or completeness. The real-world meanings are a constructed scenario.

prompts.prompt: If a candidate fails, have we proved the target underivable?
prompts.answer: No. A failed written attempt says nothing by itself about all possible derivations. Here a separate valid chain witnesses Γ⊢r.

prompts.prompt: Can the proof be valid while the selected-world target is false?
prompts.answer: Yes. If that world does not satisfy every premise, entailment makes no promise about the target there. Syntactic checking still depends on formulas and earlier citations.

Discrete samples count consecutive accepted lines at each whole revealed prefix. Failed candidates stop at three; the valid chain reaches five. The selected-step ring does not interpolate fractional proof lines. This count is not a truth value or a likelihood.
